articles.title: Is this $450 laptop from an unknown brand too good to be true?
articles.summary: The Chuwi UniBook is a fairly unknown laptop poised at undercutting the MacBook Neo with an aluminum build, Intel Wildcat Lake chip, and $449 price. But it cuts too much.
articles.body: Finding a good laptop under $500 was hard enough before RAMageddon. They nearly always had cheap hardware and underpowered, often outdated chips. That’s what made the MacBook Neo so disruptive: It offered great build quality and good-enough performance starting at $599. Windows laptops couldn’t touch it. Even though it’s gone up to $699, it’s still the laptop to beat. So when little-known Chinese brand Chuwi announced a $450 Windows laptop with an aluminum build and a brand-new Intel Wildcat Lake processor, it sounded too good to be true. It is. [Product: Chuwi UniBook | https://us.chuwi.com/products/unibook-laptop-intel-core-3-304-series-3-wildcat-lake] The UniBook comes in one configuration: a 14-inch with an Intel Core 3 304 processor, 8GB of soldered RAM, and a user-swappable 256GB SSD. That’s the lowest-end of Intel’s new Wildcat Lake chips, with just five CPU cores: one performance core, and four low-power efficiency cores. And the integrated graphics? A single GPU core. The MacBook Neo’s A18 Pro is a six-core CPU / five-core GPU ensemble, and it’s a hot rod by comparison. --- Component report card * Screen: D * Webcam: D * Keyboard: C * Trackpad: F * Port selection: A * Speakers: F * Number of ugly stickers to remove: 1 --- The UniBook feels sluggish in anything beyond basic web browsing, emails, and messaging. Its benchmark scores confirm how woefully underpowered that chip is. The MacBook Neo trounces it across the board: both single and multicore CPU performance, as well as graphics. Our Adobe Premiere 4K export test took over an hour on the UniBook. (Although at least it didn’t crash out.) I know it isn’t designed for video editing, but neither is the MacBook Neo, and the Neo exports the same video in under 10 minutes. The one edge the UniBook has is a slightly faster SSD. But despite faster storage, the UniBook’s 8GB of RAM is still a hindrance on Windows 11. It didn’t randomly lag like the recent 13-inch Surface Laptop did, but it isn’t hard to overwhelm. As on the 8GB Surface, Windows 11 uses anywhere from 4.6 to over 5GB of memory on the UniBook after a fresh reboot with no additional apps running. Once you open a half dozen Chrome tabs, a couple messaging apps, and a music streaming app, memory usage easily climbs to 7GB.  It’s no surprise Chrome crashed on me a couple times when I pushed it further with over 20 tabs across multiple virtual desktops. This is no problem on Windows laptops with 16GB of RAM, and even the MacBook Neo could handle more before slowing down. And you can count on everything moving like molasses during big file transfers. It couldn’t even load the Start menu or open the calculator app while importing photos into Lightroom Classic until the RAM and SSD bottlenecks eased.  [Image: Simple looks. Frustrating use. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/268691_Chuwi_UniBook_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0011.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] Even if your computing needs are minimal, the Chuwi’s hardware makes every interaction unpleasant. The screen is washed out, covering just 64 percent of the sRGB color space, and at 300 nits it’s pretty dim. But the worst offender is the trackpad. It’s incredibly stiff to click. You have to press it so hard the whole chassis flexes a little under the pressure. You don’t have to click the trackpad; it can detect taps too, but I never like the loosey-goosey feel of tapping — especially when executing right-clicks or click-and-drags. Using this trackpad made me physically and mentally tired. And clicking around on a laptop? Pretty important! The speakers are an affront to any music you play, as well as anyone else within earshot. They’re a tinny mess. The phone in your pocket has fuller sound. The 720p webcam is only a smidge better, but it’s still offensive to your face (and possibly your self-confidence). It’s almost passable in the best lighting, but it’s low-res, with a green color cast. In dim or backlit lighting you become a dark blur. After a few days, colleagues started greeting me in meetings with, “Oh, you must be on the Chuwi.” It’s like being told “Wow, you look tired.” “Uhh, yeah. Nice to see you too.”  [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/268691_Chuwi_UniBook_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0006.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/268691_Chuwi_UniBook_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0007.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/268691_Chuwi_UniBook_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0002.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] Amid all these downsides, there are a few bright spots. The UniBook does at least have good battery life. It easily lasts up to 10 hours on battery while doing the lightest of work: writing emails, casually browsing the web, and opening the occasional PDF. And the keyboard isn’t bad. It’s backlit, which is a genuine advantage over the MacBook Neo. It’s fine to type on, but the Neo’s and many other Windows keyboards out there feel less spongy. Also, a lack of function lock means adjusting brightness, volume, or media playback always requires a two-key combo. Not a huge deal, but a strange omission of a usual mainstay. The one thing about the UniBook that genuinely surprised me, aside from the initial reverse sticker shock, was its amount of ports. This little thing has five total USB ports, HDMI-out, microSD, and even an ethernet jack. You might expect all that on a massive gaming laptop, not a thin-and-light. But sadly, none of the USBs are faster than 5Gbps, and the HDMI is just 1.4b — topping out at a stuttery 30Hz at 4K. Any money spent on peripherals to offset the Chuwi’s shortcomings would be better spent on a different laptop. I’ve started testing a $500-ish HP OmniBook 3, and coming from the Chuwi, it was a huge relief. Even its cheap-as-they-get Snapdragon X chip offers eight cores, buoyed by twice the RAM and storage of the Chuwi, and that processor already proved it had exceptional battery life when I reviewed it in the Lenovo IdeaPad Slim 3x.  [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/268691_Chuwi_UniBook_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0008.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/268691_Chuwi_UniBook_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0012.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/268691_Chuwi_UniBook_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0009.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] I wasn’t overly impressed with the Acer Aspire 14 AI, which you can often get around $600, when I pitted it and the IdeaPad against the MacBook Neo, but it’s way better than the Chuwi for $155 more. Its Intel Lunar Lake chip gets good battery life and is powerful enough to play indie games and last-gen 3D titles on ultra-low settings. It has twice the RAM and storage as the Chuwi and nearly as many ports, and the Acer’s ports are much faster. I take no joy in telling you the Chuwi UniBook is bad and frustrating to use. I want to see decent cheap laptops, and I’m all for them coming from lesser-known brands. But Chuwi’s upstart status also brings long-term customer support into question — it doesn’t seem to have US customer service and repair centers like bigger laptop makers. And in early 2026, the company was found to have shipped laptops and mini PCs with older AMD chips disguised as newer, faster ones (even at the BIOS level). Chuwi eventually put out a statement blaming a “production error” and offered refunds for a limited time, but the situation does not inspire confidence. [Image: It’s a shame the UniBook is uniformly bad. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/268691_Chuwi_UniBook_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0003.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] The UniBook doesn’t leave a great first impression, but I want to remain hopeful that better things are on the horizon — if not for Chuwi, then at least for the Wildcat Lake processor family. Most of the major laptop makers are launching budget laptops with higher-end Wildcat Lake chips to try to compete with the Neo. Microsoft also claims it’s working on improving Windows 11’s performance with 8GB of RAM — which these new laptops desperately need. With laptop prices skyrocketing due to the RAM and storage crunch, we could all use a win. But the UniBook isn’t it. --- Chuwi UniBook specs (as reviewed) * Display: 14-inch 1920 x 1200 60Hz IPS LCD, 300 nits, anti-glare * CPU: Intel Core 3 304 (Wildcat Lake, 5 cores) * GPU: Integrated Intel Graphics * RAM: 8GB LPDDR5 (soldered) * Storage: 256GB M.2 2280 (user-accessible) * Webcam: 720p with physical privacy shutter * Connectivity: Wi-Fi 6, Bluetooth 5.2 * Ports: 2x USB-C 3.2 Gen 1 (5Gbps), 2x USB-A 3.2 Gen 1 (5Gbps), 1x USB-A 2.0 (480Mbps), HDMI 1.4b, RJ-45 gigabit ethernet, microSD card slot, 3.5mm audio jack * Biometrics: none (lockscreen password only) * Weight: 2.66 pounds / 1.2kg * Dimensions: 12.38 x 8.7 x 0.65 inches / 314.5 x 221 x 16.4mm * Battery: 53.38Wh (65W USB-C charger included) * Price: $449 --- Photography by Antonio G. articles.title: Apple is considering a screen-free wearable.
articles.summary:
With the success of Whoop and other screen-free fitness bands like the Fitbit Air, Polar Loop, and Helio Strap, it’s not a surprise that the company is weighing its options. But nothing is set in stone yet. According to Mark Gurman:
> The company is considering new devices with no displays, as well as different types of screens and various sizes. While unlikely to hit the market, round screens have even been considered. I’m told the work also includes potentially adding premium models beyond the Ultra and Hermès variants. On the lower end, Apple is considering more affordable concepts besides the current SE model.

articles.title: This great retro-inspired keyboard now comes preassembled
articles.summary: The Classic-TKL is one of my favorite keyboard kits, and now you don’t have to build it yourself
articles.body: You probably know just by looking at it if the Classic-TKL Underscore Edition is for you. Do you want a retro-looking wired keyboard without a number pad? Great. Do you care that it doesn’t have wireless? Perfect. Do you want it preassembled? Buddy, you’re in the right place.  But Nathan, you might say, preassembled is the regular way to buy a keyboard. That is the baseline expectation. Most people buying a cake expect a cake, not a box of cake mix. And that’s true, for most people and most keyboards. But until now, the Classic-TKL has only been available as a bare-bones kit, and now you can buy one ready to go, with quality components, for less than the price of doing a similar build yourself.  If you’re like me, figuring out what keycaps, switches, and stabilizers to use, then putting them all together, is a big part of the fun of mechanical keyboards. But if you just want something to type with that looks retro and sounds and feels nice, without having to build it yourself — or if you were going to use classic beige keycaps anyway — then the Underscore Edition might be up your alley.  [Product: NovelKeys Classic-TKL Underscore Edition | https://novelkeys.com/pages/classic-tkl-underscore] The $189 NovelKeys Classic-TKL Underscore Edition is a wired-only, gasket-mounted tenkeyless mechanical keyboard. It has an injection-molded plastic case with a high forehead, reminiscent of the 18-year-old Realforce 86U, and a silicone mat on the base for sound dampening. It also has hot-swap MX switches, full RGB backlighting, and a light bar (both of which can be turned off), and it’s fully programmable using the Via web app.  The Classic-TKL has been around for a couple of years in kit form. I built one and wrote about it in 2024; I also tested the glow-in-the-dark version. I like them a lot! But apparently not everyone who wants a nice retro-looking keyboard also wants a craft project. Michael Sickler, who owns NovelKeys, told me that the Underscore Edition is aimed at giving NovelKeys’ keyboard enthusiast customer base something they can recommend to friends and family. It’s also aimed at professionals who might lurk on the keyboard subreddits and Discords enough to know what they want, but don’t want to build it themselves. (This is basically the same thing Ryan Norbauer told me about his Seneca, except the Seneca is 20 times more expensive.)   [Image: From the top: boulder, lichen, and clay. I tested the clay but look at that green. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/classic-tkl_colors.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] The Underscore Edition comes in clay (warm beige), boulder (taupe-ish), and lichen (a dusty green). My review unit is clay, but I’d buy the lichen personally. It ships with NovelKeys’ own Classic Blue switches, GMK CYL Classic Beige keycaps, a USB A-to-C cable, and preinstalled and pretuned TypePlus stabilizers. These are name-brand parts. GMK CYL keycaps are the benchmark for doubleshot Cherry-profile keycaps. They’re several steps in quality above the keycaps that come with a Keychron, for example. The letters and numbers are crisp and clear and the consistency is unmatched. They’re also expensive; you’d pay at least $120 if you bought them on their own, though you would get more keycaps. The Classic-TKL comes with just the ones you need to cover the board. [Image: Nice thick doubleshot keycaps and smooth switches. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/268660_Classic-TKL_keyboard_AKrales_0110.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] The TypePlus stabilizers are also a good choice; I’ve installed and tuned a couple sets myself, but the people who made them do a better job. There’s no rattle or tick on any of the stabilized keys. And the Classic Blue linear switches (also made by TypePlus) are also nice. They’re smooth and stable, with almost no wobble; at 53g actuation force and 63g bottom-out, they’re medium-heavy, like a lighter version of the Cherry MX Blacks in my first-ever mechanical keyboard in 2009. They’re not silent, but they’re also not as loud as you’d expect a keyboard this beige to be. (I still feel like a blue switch should be clicky, though.)  I try to avoid the “fans of the genre” review. You know, “if this is the kind of thing you like, you’re going to like it.” But once you get past the strictly utilitarian, pretty much everything about mechanical keyboards comes down to preference and taste.  The Classic-TKL Underscore Edition is a well-executed version of what it is. If you want an earth-tone retro-looking tenkeyless board — a classic TKL, if you will — with linear switches and beige Cherry-profile keycaps, it’s a great choice.  [Image: It has a nice side profile. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/268660_Classic-TKL_keyboard_AKrales_0169.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] When you think of it as a high-quality preassembled version of an enthusiast DIY keyboard, with name-brand parts, it’s also a good deal. I built the DIY version of the same board with the same stabilizers and similarly priced keycaps in September 2024. It worked out to $276, and took me an hour to put together (most of which was spent lubing and tuning the stabilizers). The Underscore Edition costs $189, $100 more than the bare-bones kit. You can’t get keycaps, switches, and stabilizers of this quality for $100 combined. But it’s also true that $189 can get you a lot of keyboard these days, especially if you’re not attached to the Classic-TKL’s particular vibe.  Even within the tenkeyless form factor, the Evoworks Evo80 costs $169 and comes with an aluminum case and both Bluetooth and 2.4GHz wireless. Same for the $179 Wobkey Crush 80. But those are different keyboards, with different aesthetics. The 8BitDo Retro 87 is closer, with several classic-computing-inspired flavors including Commodore 64 and IBM Model M, for around $100. But — no disrespect to the 8BitDo here — those look maybe a smidge more casual than the Classic-TKL. I prefer the Classic-TKL’s plastic chassis to the aluminum of the Evoworks or Wobkey boards. But I wouldn’t mind if it had wireless. It’d also be nice if it shipped with a few extra keycaps, in case you want Mac legends or Control in its proper place (Caps Lock). While I’m being picky: I also wish it came with the option for MTNU Classic Beige keycaps, rather than just CYL, because I like MTNU better. An electrocapacitive switch option would be nice too, but now I’m just getting greedy. (Actually, now I’m just reinventing the Realforce.)  If you want the Classic-TKL in a different color, or with different switches or keycaps, there’s still the kit version and the Glo version. And if you want a different keyboard entirely, well, those abound. The Classic-TKL Underscore Edition is the thing that it is, and it’s good at that.  I’d still go for the green one, though. Photography by Amelia Holowaty Krales / The Verge except where noted.

articles.title: Google’s Pixel 11 series pairs a little new hardware with a lot of new software
articles.summary: More helpful features, less AI slop.
articles.body: When I first picked up the Pixel 11 Pro this week, it was clear to me that this was one of those refinement years — at least when it comes to hardware. Aesthetically, the phones are as beautiful as ever, with Google’s signature camera bar and bright, colorful backing glass. There are small updates, like a single piece of glass covering the camera bar and the all-new HiLight ambient LED on the Pros. But this year, the Pixel is all about quality of life and software improvements. After weeks of teasers, Google has finally formally announced the Pixel 11, Pixel 11 Pro, Pixel 11 Pro XL, and Pixel 11 Pro Fold. The phones are all shipping next week, on August 20th, and Google is holding a splashy event the evening of August 12th to show off the devices. Ahead of that, we had a chance to take a first look at everything that’s coming up. Pixel 11 [Image: The standard Pixel 11 gets some bold colors this year. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/Google-Pixel-11-Hot-pink.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] Let’s start with the bad news up front: All of these phones are $100 more expensive than last year’s. Google has killed off the 128GB base storage option this year, which means the Pixel 11 now starts at $899 for a 256GB model. All storage tiers still come with 12GB of RAM, but the higher entry price is no doubt driven by RAMageddon, which has been increasing costs across the industry. If you can look past the price, you’ll find a refined version of last year’s phone that looks and feels a bit more premium. The camera bar is now made of a singular piece of glass and is over 40 percent thinner. If you use it with one of Google’s cases, the bar will become completely flush. (This gives you three different camera bar thickness options on the Pixel line now, which only get thicker the more premium you go.) [Image: The camera bump difference between the Pixel 11 and Pixel 11 Pro. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/Google-Pixel-11-vs-Pro-camera-bump-comparison.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] The cameras have been upgraded, too. On the Pixel 11, the 48MP wide is quoted with 56 percent more light gathering capability from its new 1/1.56-inch sensor, and the 5x telephoto lens can now digitally zoom up to 30x, which Google says is enabled by the new image signal processor in the Tensor G6 chipset. And considering the new Tensor G6 chip is said to be up to 20 percent more efficient, Google is quoting up to 30-plus hours of battery life across the lineup. Perhaps the most interesting update to me is the new Camera Looks feature. You can think of this similarly to the film recipes on Fujifilm cameras, presenting users with stylized presets that can be customized to their liking.  [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/Pixel-11-Pro-Editorial-camera-look.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/Pixel-11-Pro-Minimal-camera-look.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all] What makes Camera Looks so interesting, though, is instead of just being a filter on top of the preprocessed Pixel photo, the phone will process the photo completely differently at the sensor level depending on which settings you choose, potentially using less frame stacking and sharpening to deliver the photo you actually want. During my briefing at least, this really delivered. The Natural mode does an amazing job of lowering the sharpness and contrast and making the photos look much more true to life, and I’m excited to take it for a proper spin later. If you want to learn more about this, check out my dedicated article where I spoke with Pixel camera lead Isaac Reynolds. Another new feature inside the camera is Magic Capture. This is a camera mode alongside the photo and video modes that creates a sort of hybrid mashup of the two, where the phone will automatically pick out short clips and images you can share. During my hands-on time this feature didn’t work great, only giving me one small clip and one photo from a roughly 15-second recording, but I believe it’s meant for longer clips at things like kids’ birthday parties. We’ll have to test this in the field once we have more time with the device. [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/Google-Pixel-11-Magic-Capture-2.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/Google-Pixel-11-Creator-Suite-2.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] Google is also adding a new Creator Suite inside the camera, which gives you access to tools like social media framing guides, speech enhancement, a teleprompter, and automatic folder structures for video. I was surprised to see this so deeply integrated into the camera itself, and it’s clear Google is going after a new audience and hoping to make the Pixel the best phone for small creators. The phones also all feature Qi2.2 — an upgrade from Qi2 last year. Google says this offers 25 percent faster wireless charging of up to 25W, an upgrade from the 15W max the Pixel 10 offered. However, many users reported seeing a maximum wireless charge rate of only 5W with the Pixel 10 when using older chargers, so hopefully the problem is fixed this year. The Pixel 11 will come in purple, green, black, and an extremely hot magenta. Pixel 11 Pro and Pro XL [Image: The Pixel 11 Pro in blue. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/Google-Pixel-11-Pro-back-of-phone-in-hand.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] The 11 Pro and Pro XL are where things get a little more interesting this year. Like the standard Pixel 11, they start at 256GB of storage and 12GB of RAM (down from 16GB last year), which starts at $1,099. If you’re a power user, you can still get 16GB of RAM if you buy the 512GB or 1TB models. You’re definitely getting more with the Pro models this year, though. The display on the Pixel 11 Pro gets up to a super bright 3,600 nits, which Google says is the brightest display ever on a smartphone. This isn’t a massive difference from the 3,300-nit peak brightness from last year, but it’s something for your money. [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/Google-Pixel-11-Pro-screen-head-on.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/Google-Pixel-11-Pro-Pixel-Glow-Macro-2.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] The main camera sensor on the Pixel 11 Pro has been improved, with a new 50MP model that Google says uses less power and should perform better in the 1x-to-5x zoom range. There’s also a new 48MP telephoto lens with a larger 1/1.95-inch sensor that delivers a quoted 30 percent improvement in light sensitivity. And just like the standard Pixel 11, the 11 Pro has a further zoom range, now extending up to 120x, which Google says is enabled by the ISP in Tensor G6. On the Pro phones, Google has also substantially sped up Night Sight, offering up to 4.5x faster low-light image capture, though Google tells me on average it’s about 3x faster than last year. This is still a pretty substantial improvement, and Reynolds told me the idea was to optimize Night Sight for handheld capture. “You can still capture for up to four minutes if you want all the light,” he tells me, “but it’s really optimized for those awkward moments where you have to tell someone to hold still for a little too long.” [Image: The HiLight LED replaces the old temperature sensor. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/Google-Pixel-11-Pro-Pixel-Glow-Macro.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] The flashiest feature (pun intended) of the new Pro phones is the HiLight feature. Pixel 11 Pro and Pro Fold phones now feature an RGB LED ring where the temperature sensor used to be on the right side of the camera bar. When you’re talking to Gemini, the LED will glow blue as it listens and responds to you. Separately, you can set favorite contacts to glow when they call you through the default Phone app or WhatsApp. Google is marketing the feature as a way to be more present in your everyday life, but it doesn’t feel particularly useful to me yet considering its use is so limited. Google says more functionality is coming in the future, but right now, this doesn’t feel like a reason to buy the phone. The Pixel 11 Pro and Pro XL will come in olive, light blue, and a striking orange-ish “canyon” color, all with glossy side rails. There’s also a black option, which this year has matte side rails, unlike all the other Pro devices. Pixel 11 Pro Fold [Image: The Pixel 11 Pro Fold in olive. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/Google-Pixel-11-Pro-Fold-closed-in-hands.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] Finally, there’s the Pixel 11 Pro Fold. Google is calling it the most durable Pixel Fold yet, with a new composite back material that Google says is nearly impossible to crack. This, alongside a thicker inner ultra-thin glass display, contributes to Google’s “3x more durable” claim compared to last year. The inner bezels have also been reduced, making it Google’s thinnest Fold bezels ever, and the peak brightness matches the Pixel 11 Pro at 3,600 nits. The 11 Pro Fold is also inheriting the new 48MP main sensor from the Pixel 11 for a quoted 56 percent improved light sensitivity compared to last year, and it gets Qi2.2 for up to 20 percent faster wireless charging. The 11 Pro Fold starts at 16GB of RAM standard with 256GB of storage, comes in olive and black, and starts at $1,899 — also a $100 price jump over last year. Photography by David Imel / The Verge

On the Pixel 11, the 48MP wide is quoted with 56 percent more light gathering capability from its new 1/1.56-inch sensor, and the 5x telephoto lens can now digitally zoom up to 30x, which Google says is enabled by the new image signal processor in the Tensor G6 chipset. And considering the new Tensor G6 chip is said to be up to 20 percent more efficient, Google is quoting up to 30-plus hours of battery life across the lineup. Perhaps the most interesting update to me is the new Camera Looks feature. You can think of this similarly to the film recipes on Fujifilm cameras, presenting users with stylized presets that can be customized to their liking.  [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/Pixel-11-Pro-Editorial-camera-look.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/Pixel-11-Pro-Minimal-camera-look.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all] What makes Camera Looks so interesting, though, is instead of just being a filter on top of the preprocessed Pixel photo, the phone will process the photo completely differently at the sensor level depending on which settings you choose, potentially using less frame stacking and sharpening to deliver the photo you actually want. During my briefing at least, this really delivered. The Natural mode does an amazing job of lowering the sharpness and contrast and making the photos look much more true to life, and I’m excited to take it for a proper spin later. We’ll have to test this in the field once we have more time with the device. I was surprised to see this so deeply integrated into the camera itself, and it’s clear Google is going after a new audience and hoping to make the Pixel the best phone for small creators. The phones also all feature Qi2.2 — an upgrade from Qi2 last year. Google says this offers 25 percent faster wireless charging of up to 25W, an upgrade from the 15W max the Pixel 10 offered. However, many users reported seeing a maximum wireless charge rate of only 5W with the Pixel 10 when using older chargers, so hopefully the problem is fixed this year. The Pixel 11 will come in purple, green, black, and an extremely hot magenta. Pixel 11 Pro and Pro XL [Image: The Pixel 11 Pro in blue. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/Google-Pixel-11-Pro-back-of-phone-in-hand.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] The 11 Pro and Pro XL are where things get a little more interesting this year. Like the standard Pixel 11, they start at 256GB of storage and 12GB of RAM (down from 16GB last year), which starts at $1,099. If you’re a power user, you can still get 16GB of RAM if you buy the 512GB or 1TB models. You’re definitely getting more with the Pro models this year, though. The display on the Pixel 11 Pro gets up to a super bright 3,600 nits, which Google says is the brightest display ever on a smartphone. This isn’t a massive difference from the 3,300-nit peak brightness from last year, but it’s something for your money. [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/Google-Pixel-11-Pro-screen-head-on.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/Google-Pixel-11-Pro-Pixel-Glow-Macro-2.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] The main camera sensor on the Pixel 11 Pro has been improved, with a new 50MP model that Google says uses less power and should perform better in the 1x-to-5x zoom range. There’s also a new 48MP telephoto lens with a larger 1/1.95-inch sensor that delivers a quoted 30 percent improvement in light sensitivity. And just like the standard Pixel 11, the 11 Pro has a further zoom range, now extending up to 120x, which Google says is enabled by the ISP in Tensor G6. On the Pro phones, Google has also substantially sped up Night Sight, offering up to 4.5x faster low-light image capture, though Google tells me on average it’s about 3x faster than last year. This is still a pretty substantial improvement, and Reynolds told me the idea was to optimize Night Sight for handheld capture. “You can still capture for up to four minutes if you want all the light,” he tells me, “but it’s really optimized for those awkward moments where you have to tell someone to hold still for a little too long.” [Image: The HiLight LED replaces the old temperature sensor. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/Google-Pixel-11-Pro-Pixel-Glow-Macro.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] The flashiest feature (pun intended) of the new Pro phones is the HiLight feature. Pixel 11 Pro and Pro Fold phones now feature an RGB LED ring where the temperature sensor used to be on the right side of the camera bar. When you’re talking to Gemini, the LED will glow blue as it listens and responds to you. Separately, you can set favorite contacts to glow when they call you through the default Phone app or WhatsApp. Google is marketing the feature as a way to be more present in your everyday life, but it doesn’t feel particularly useful to me yet considering its use is so limited. Google says more functionality is coming in the future, but right now, this doesn’t feel like a reason to buy the phone. The Pixel 11 Pro and Pro XL will come in olive, light blue, and a striking orange-ish “canyon” color, all with glossy side rails. There’s also a black option, which this year has matte side rails, unlike all the other Pro devices. Pixel 11 Pro Fold [Image: The Pixel 11 Pro Fold in olive. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/Google-Pixel-11-Pro-Fold-closed-in-hands.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] Finally, there’s the Pixel 11 Pro Fold. Google is calling it the most durable Pixel Fold yet, with a new composite back material that Google says is nearly impossible to crack. This, alongside a thicker inner ultra-thin glass display, contributes to Google’s “3x more durable” claim compared to last year. The inner bezels have also been reduced, making it Google’s thinnest Fold bezels ever, and the peak brightness matches the Pixel 11 Pro at 3,600 nits. The 11 Pro Fold is also inheriting the new 48MP main sensor from the Pixel 11 for a quoted 56 percent improved light sensitivity compared to last year, and it gets Qi2.2 for up to 20 percent faster wireless charging. The 11 Pro Fold starts at 16GB of RAM standard with 256GB of storage, comes in olive and black, and starts at $1,899 — also a $100 price jump over last year. Photography by David Imel / The Verge

articles.title: Don’t overlook Elektron’s budget electronic music instruments
articles.summary: Elektron’s Model:Samples and Model:Cycles are criminally slept-on electronic music instruments that are more powerful and fun than their bargain price suggests.
articles.body:
When I’m asked what to buy if you want to get into making electronic music, I often recommend Elektron’s budget-minded Model:Samples and Model:Cycles grooveboxes. They don’t grab headlines the way Teenage Engineering’s gear or the Telepathic Instruments Orchid do, and even compared to the company’s higher-end and more niche musical offerings like the Digitakt, Octatrack, or Tonverk, they’re often overlooked. But as my collection has grown to include fancier and far more expensive instruments, I still find myself coming back to the Model series. Those looking to get their first groovebox are often drawn to more familiar brand names like Korg or Roland. And lots of people on Reddit will be quick to recommend the Novation Circuit Tracks (which I personally find confusing and mediocre-sounding). This is probably also partially due to the reputation Elektron gear has for being obtuse. If you’re an established music maker and aren’t deterred by a complicated workflow, you’re probably going to pick up a more powerful Elektron box, like the Digitone or Syntakt. That leaves the Models lineup in a weird no man’s land, and that’s a shame. The primary difference between the two Models instruments is that the Model:Cycles uses FM synthesis and the Model:Samples, appropriately enough, plays samples. (It is not technically a sampler, however, since it can’t record samples, and instead they have to be loaded over USB.)  [Image: Connectivity isn’t the Model:Cycles’ strong suit. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/elektron-model-cycles-model-samples-5.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] The Model:Cycles is built around a streamlined version of the engine found in the Digitone, one of my favorite-sounding synths of all time. This is a modern take on FM that can do the cold bells and icy pads you associate with iconic instruments like the DX7 (the iconic sound of the ’80s). But it also does modern glassy keys and aggressive turn-of-the-millennium EDM bass. The two are more alike than not, though. They’re both six-track grooveboxes with six velocity-sensitive pads and plenty of knobs for hands-on controls, and they look almost identical. But most importantly, they feature Elektron’s legendary step sequencer without being nearly as intimidating as the company’s more expensive and notoriously complicated offerings. The sequencer is built around what the company calls “trigs” and “locks.” Trigs are basically just events, typically triggering a note, and locks are just step-specific settings. It seems like a simple enough concept, but it makes these instruments far more capable than they might seem at first blush. ---

--- Six tracks isn’t a lot to work with. Once you’ve loaded up a kick, snare, and hi-hat, then you’ve only got three more tracks for bass, any melodic elements, and additional percussion. But sound locks allow you to change samples or presets on a per-step basis. That means, so long as they never play simultaneously, you can have your kick and snare share the same track, then you can put your hi-hats and other percussion on a second track, and leave the four other tracks for everything else. This is just the most obvious example of how locks expand the possibilities of what might seem rather limited on paper. The sequencer can be treated like a simple step sequencer where you drop a four-on-the-floor kick and a snare on the backbeat. But it also grows with you as your skills improve, and you want to create more complex tracks. Trig conditions, for example, allow you to set rules that govern when certain steps are triggered, like only every third time through the loop, only when you press the fill button, or only if a previous trig condition is met. This means that you can create a huge amount of variety in a single 64-step pattern. And then you can chain several of those patterns together to create complex and evolving arrangements that just aren’t possible on most gear in this price range. [Image: There’s plenty of hands-on controls for jamming. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/elektron-model-cycles-model-samples-7.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] The Models boxes are also just incredibly fun. Where Elektron’s other gear demands a lot of menu diving, the Model:Samples and Model:Cycles are immediately approachable and built for live performance. It’s easy to trigger a drum fill with the push of a button, tweak a knob to open the filter on a bass, or briefly bathe a lead melody in delay.  Control-all might be the most fun feature, which, as you might have guessed, allows you to control all the tracks simultaneously. Bury your entire track in reverb as you start cranking up the distortion and lowering the pitch of all your samples to create a mangled, chaotic breakdown. And then immediately undo it all and drop the beat again by pressing the function and pattern buttons. The Model:Samples and Model:Cycles encourage jamming in a way that frankly a lot of electronic music gear just doesn’t, and it’s an absolute blast. Now, they’re not without their flaws. The pads are pretty mediocre. Having to load samples via USB rather than recording them directly kinda sucks. And the lack of polyphony (each sequencer track can only play one note at a time) is a bit of a bummer. But at $349, it’s hard to complain. Plus they can be snagged used for as little as $200 on Reverb or Craigslist. Frankly, they’re some of the best bargains in music hardware and a great place to start your journey into producing electronic music.

articles.title: Sonos finally added Live Activities controls for your iPhone lockscreen
articles.summary: The latest update to the Sonos app adds support for iOS Live Activities, putting basic controls and info on your lockscreen.
articles.body: Sonos released an update to its mobile app that finally introduces support for iOS’ Live Activities, giving iPhone users quick access to playback controls on their lockscreen. The added functionality is a “much requested, anticipated, and needed feature,” according to a post Sonos shared to Reddit today that was spotted by 9to5Mac. While some features like displaying album art are not available, the Sonos Live Activity provides basic details and controls when listening to music or podcasts through a Sonos system without having to fully unlock your iPhone and open the app.  Support for Live Activities and lockscreen controls similar to what’s already available in the Android version of the Sonos app was teased by the company’s CEO Tom Conrad during an interview with Bloomberg last February. And following backlash to a major Sonos app update in 2024, support for Live Activities is off by default but can be enabled by navigating to both the Sonos app’s preferences as well as the Sonos app section of iOS’ settings. Once it’s turned on, the Live Activity will appear “after you initiate playback and then close the app” and displays the name of the group or room where audio was last playing from and the title of what you’re listening to. After playback stops, the Live Activity will automatically disappear from your lockscreen after 15 minutes. Support for the Apple Watch and CarPlay is included, but while the Live Activity will be displayed on your wrist or in your car, the controls aren’t supported there. It’s not known if or when those controls will ever work, but Sonos says its team is still working to improve the new feature, and when it comes to album art, the company is exploring “alternative ways to enhance the lock screen experience.”

articles.title: Apple’s camera-equipped AirPods appear in leaked video
articles.summary: We may have our first glimpse of Apple’s rumored camera-equipped AirPods, thanks to a demo video pulled from the macOS Tahoe 26.7 Release Candidate.
articles.body: We may have our first glimpse of Apple’s rumored camera-equipped AirPods, thanks to a video that MacRumors found in the macOS Tahoe 26.7 Release Candidate. The short video clip features a man — who is wearing the new AirPods — holding up a book with the cover displayed, so that Visual Intelligence can see the book title.  A Siri voice-over plays over the clip, saying “with Visual Intelligence, your world becomes savable. See something you like? Just ask me to save it for later.” Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman has previously reported that the rumored AirPods with cameras are designed to take in “visual information in low resolution” and act as eyes for Apple’s AI features, potentially allowing Siri to give turn-by-turn directions or answer questions about the wearer’s surroundings. The AirPods shown in the new demo clip look like a slightly thicker version of the AirPods Pro 3. That’s what Gurman had predicted, along with longer stems to accommodate the cameras, and LED lights that indicate when data is being uploaded to the cloud. We only get a look at the AirPods from the back in the video, but no lights can be seen on them from that angle. [Media: https://twitter.com/aaronp613/status/2089522745184760112] Given those Visual Intelligence features, the AirPods are poised to compete with other camera-equipped AI gadgets like Meta’s Ray-Ban smart glasses, though Apple is also reportedly working on its own smart glasses too. While the AirPods’ cameras “aren’t designed” to snap photos or videos, the stealthy form factor may exacerbate the existing privacy concerns surrounding camera-equipped AI products, following Meta’s “pervert glasses” backlash. For now, details about Apple’s AirPods with cameras are still slim. If demo videos are already making their way into Apple’s OS betas, the new AirPods may launch alongside the improved version of Siri, which is expected to arrive in September together with the next generation of iPhones.

articles.title: Amazon Fire TV devices are getting a free Alexa Plus upgrade
articles.summary: Amazon is bringing its upgraded Alexa Plus AI assistant to all Fire TV device owners in the US for free.
articles.body: Amazon is bringing Alexa Plus to Fire TV device owners in the US for free. Starting today, users in the US with an Amazon Fire TV Stick, Fire TV Cube, Amazon Ember smart TV, or other TV with Alexa Plus built in, including those from Panasonic and Hisense, will get access to the more conversational AI assistant. Previously, Amazon made Alexa Plus available to Fire TV customers with a Prime or Alexa Plus subscription. But now, everyone will get access to Alexa Plus, which can provide movie recommendations based on your mood, help you jump to specific scenes, and answer questions about what you’re seeing onscreen. It can also connect to your smart home devices, allowing you to control lighting, door locks, pull up camera feeds, and more. Amazon says it will automatically upgrade all Fire TV owners to Alexa Plus. The company adds that it “additional devices and regions may be added over time.”

articles.title: Google’s Pixel 11 Pro Fold feels like the end of an era
articles.summary: Google’s Pixel 11 Pro Fold is a great foldable, with IP68 and a reliable triple camera, trapped in a shape everyone else seems to be moving on from.
articles.body: The foldable phone market is in the middle of a huge transformation, but no one told Google. Last year, Samsung transformed its Galaxy Z Fold 7 with a dramatically thinner design. This year, it made its phones thinner and lighter again, almost eliminated the crease, and introduced a new passport-sized form factor that feels like the future. Next month, Apple is expected to enter the market with a foldable iPhone that, rumor has it, includes all of the above and adds iOS too. In the face of all that flux, Google’s Pixel 11 Pro Fold has hardly changed a thing. Like the other Pixel 11 phones, this is an iterative hardware upgrade, but unlike the others its design feels dated already. It’s a little thinner and lighter than last year’s phone, the main camera is a bit better, the screens a touch brighter. But it’s mostly the same hardware, boosted by software updates like Camera Looks, multitasking Bubbles, and Creator Suite tools.  This isn’t a bad phone at all. The IP68 rating makes it tougher than Samsung’s latest, and the triple camera and solid software are both big draws. Perhaps not changing the design will even work in Google’s favor: The 11 Pro Fold’s aspect ratio sits in between the two extremes of Samsung’s 2026 lineup, its stocky Z Fold 8 and skinny Z Fold 8 Ultra, and despite a price hike still feels competitively priced with either. That’s enough to mean the 11 Pro Fold still feels like a smart purchase right now, but I’m worried it won’t do for long. Unlike on the other Pixel 11 models, that’s not masking a storage bump: This has the same 256GB starting storage as last year’s model. You can pay an extra $120 to get 512GB storage, and a further $230 to get 1TB. Every version comes with 16GB of RAM. That $100 hike gets you a handful of hardware improvements on last year’s phone. The chipset has been upgraded to the new Tensor G6; both OLED displays run a bit brighter, now peaking at 3,600 nits; the 48-megapixel main camera uses a larger image sensor; and the Qi2 magnetic wireless charging now runs at 25W, up from 15W. That’s just about it in terms of actual performance upgrades. There have been slightly bigger changes to the design though. This year’s phone is 0.7mm thinner when closed and weighs 19g less. That doesn’t sound like a whole lot, but holding the two generations side by side you can easily tell the difference, and the 11 Pro Fold is more comfortable to use for extended periods. Still, it might be too little. Last year, Samsung slimmed its Z Fold 7 down dramatically, and pushed that even further this year, echoing similarly slim designs from Chinese rivals Oppo and Honor. Google’s foldable still feels big and bulky by comparison, like hardware that’s a generation behind. The same is true of the display’s crease, which is pretty obvious even head-on, and easily noticeable when swiping from side to side. Oppo and Samsung have both worked miracles to make their creases almost invisible unless the light’s just right, and it feels like Google has a lot of catching up to do.  [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/google-pixel-11-pro-fold-08.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/google-pixel-11-pro-fold-09.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/google-pixel-11-pro-fold-02.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] The almost square main display is well-suited to multitasking, helped by Bubbles, a new Android 17 feature that’s available on every Pixel but comes into its own on the foldables. Multiple apps can be opened in floating bubbles, allowing quick access to a smaller window that can be minimized just as easily. On the 11 Pro Fold’s larger display, those bubbles can float perpetually in a dedicated dock in the bottom-right corner for unobtrusive access. It’s ideal for hopping into Spotify to skip a song, diving into Todoist to tick off a task, or pulling up WhatsApp to reply to a message, all before getting back to whatever you were working on. But in the wake of Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8, this square screen feels a little behind the times. The industry seems to agree: Huawei has adopted the same design, Apple is expected to, and both Honor and Oppo are rumored to have wide foldables in the works. I enjoyed Samsung’s passport-sized form factor for its pocketability and natural feel when reading or watching TV and miss it while using this. By contrast, the 11 Pro Fold is tall when closed, and boxy when open. I do find it more comfortable than the unnaturally skinny Z Fold 8 Ultra though, and anyone split between Samsung’s two shapes may find this a happy medium. [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/google-pixel-11-pro-fold-10.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/google-pixel-11-pro-fold-05.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] Still, the 11 Pro Fold has its own advantages. Unlike those phones, it has an IP68 rating for dust- and water-resistance, following the similar score on the 10 Pro Fold. For a phone that can cost upwards of $2,000, that extra level of protection is worth more than mere peace of mind. Google also boasts that the new glass fiber composite back is three times more durable and “nearly impossible to crack.” Google’s foldables remain the only ones to support Qi2 magnetic wireless charging, here upgraded to faster 25W speeds. The necessary magnets are part of why the phone is thicker than rivals, a tradeoff which will make sense for some.  This may have Qi2, but it doesn’t have a silicon-carbon battery, unlike Samsung’s new foldables. As a result, in slimming the phone, Google also shrunk the battery. The 4,806mAh capacity is only a little smaller than the 10 Pro Fold’s 5,015mAh though, and battery life itself has been fine, routinely lasting until the end of the day with a little bit to spare. This is still an all-day phone, it just isn’t especially close to being a two-day one. [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/google-pixel-11-pro-fold-04.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/google-pixel-11-pro-fold-07.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] The biggest design tweak is HiLight, Google’s attempt to reinvent the notification light by repurposing the camera flash into a multicolor LED. As a long-term notification light stan, I was excited to see Google resurrect it, but if this shambling corpse is the result, it should have stayed dead. HiLight is currently only used for two things: a multicolor glow when you talk to Gemini, and a monocolor glow when one of your favorite contacts calls. Neither works unless the phone is lying flat and face-down with the screen off, and customization is limited to a measly pool of five colors for call alerts. Support for message notifications is coming later, Google says, with no word on whether it will ever be usable for notifications at large, serve as a charging indicator, or offer deeper customizability. If HiLight was going to be this basic, why did Google even bother? More worthwhile is the single camera upgrade. The new 48-megapixel main camera sensor is the same as on the regular Pixel 11, and the two phones share matching 5x telephoto lenses too, with similar (though not identical) ultrawide and selfie cameras. Broadly speaking, the 11 Pro Fold camera is about the same as the 11’s and — on paper, at least — a step down from the Pro phones’. I won’t go into them in too much detail here, since my colleague David Imel does a great job of exactly that in his Pixel 11 Pro and Pro XL review, but I’ll give you the gist. New Camera Looks are the biggest tweak, similar to the Film Simulations popularized on Fujifilm cameras. It’s a great option when you just want to capture kids and pets in action, and aren’t too stressed about lining up a perfect shot. Then there’s the Creator Suite, a set of tools specifically designed for content creators, including an onscreen teleprompter and the option to save videos and photos directly into project folders for easier organization. [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/PXL_20260819_114909140.MC_.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/PXL_20260819_114918639.MC_.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/PXL_20260819_114934962.MC_.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] Software improvements elsewhere are focused on AI. Rambler is a dictation tool capable of interpreting meandering monologues and creating concise summaries instead. The bigger addition is Proactive Assistance, an upgraded version of Magic Cue that pops up with prompts for tasks it can help with. When it works, that is; the feature isn’t available in the UK at all, so I haven’t been able to test it, and my US-based colleagues reviewing the other Pixel 11 models found it hard to reliably trigger. With Samsung rejigging its foldable lineup, and Apple’s first foldable iPhone seemingly imminent, Google might have picked the wrong year to be iterative. I wrote in my review that Samsung’s wider Z Fold 8 feels like the future of foldables; by extension, this might be the past.  The 11 Pro Fold is far from obsolete though. This is still, for now at least, this year’s only foldable with an IP68 rating and magnetic charging. Including a triple rear camera at the same price Samsung offers a double is a major selling point, and the suite of software updates — especially Camera Looks and Bubbles — might draw me back to this phone over either recent Galaxy. Whether they’re enough to compete with whatever Apple is about to offer is another question entirely. It’s impossible for us to read and analyze every single one of these agreements. But we started counting exactly how many times you have to hit “agree” to use devices when we review them since these are agreements most people don’t read and definitely can’t negotiate. To use the Pixel 11 Pro Fold, you must agree to: * Google Terms of Service * Google Play Terms of Service * Google Privacy Policy (included in ToS) * Install apps and updates: “You agree this device may also automatically download and install updates and apps from Google, your carrier, and your device’s manufacturer, possibly using cellular data.” There’s also a variety of optional agreements, including: * Provide anonymous location data for Google’s services * “Allow apps and services to scan for Wi-Fi networks and nearby devices at any time, even when Wi-Fi or Bluetooth is off.” * Send usage and diagnostic data to Google * Google phone number verification * Google Gemini Apps Privacy Notice if you opt in to using Gemini Assistant * Google AI Prohibited Use Policy * Let contacts nearby find and share with you Other features, like Google Wallet, may require additional agreements. Final tally: four mandatory agreements and at least seven optional agreements. ---

Still, with Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8 dropping the telephoto entirely, having any third lens here — and a pretty good one, at that — is now a big boon for the Pixel foldable. Google has bolstered the camera app with a whole suite of software upgrades, which might matter more than the hardware changes. I won’t go into them in too much detail here, since my colleague David Imel does a great job of exactly that in his Pixel 11 Pro and Pro XL review, but I’ll give you the gist. New Camera Looks are the biggest tweak, similar to the Film Simulations popularized on Fujifilm cameras. There are four default looks, which subtly change the style of an image, and another six with more dramatic effects, and each can be further tweaked with direct control over contrast, vibrance, sharpness, and more. It’s a great option when you just want to capture kids and pets in action, and aren’t too stressed about lining up a perfect shot. Then there’s the Creator Suite, a set of tools specifically designed for content creators, including an onscreen teleprompter and the option to save videos and photos directly into project folders for easier organization. Rambler is a dictation tool capable of interpreting meandering monologues and creating concise summaries instead. The bigger addition is Proactive Assistance, an upgraded version of Magic Cue that pops up with prompts for tasks it can help with. When it works, that is; the feature isn’t available in the UK at all, so I haven’t been able to test it, and my US-based colleagues reviewing the other Pixel 11 models found it hard to reliably trigger. With Samsung rejigging its foldable lineup, and Apple’s first foldable iPhone seemingly imminent, Google might have picked the wrong year to be iterative. I wrote in my review that Samsung’s wider Z Fold 8 feels like the future of foldables; by extension, this might be the past.  The 11 Pro Fold is far from obsolete though. This is still, for now at least, this year’s only foldable with an IP68 rating and magnetic charging. Including a triple rear camera at the same price Samsung offers a double is a major selling point, and the suite of software updates — especially Camera Looks and Bubbles — might draw me back to this phone over either recent Galaxy. Whether they’re enough to compete with whatever Apple is about to offer is another question entirely. It’s impossible for us to read and analyze every single one of these agreements. But we started counting exactly how many times you have to hit “agree” to use devices when we review them since these are agreements most people don’t read and definitely can’t negotiate. To use the Pixel 11 Pro Fold, you must agree to: * Google Terms of Service * Google Play Terms of Service * Google Privacy Policy (included in ToS) * Install apps and updates: “You agree this device may also automatically download and install updates and apps from Google, your carrier, and your device’s manufacturer, possibly using cellular data.” There’s also a variety of optional agreements, including: * Provide anonymous location data for Google’s services * “Allow apps and services to scan for Wi-Fi networks and nearby devices at any time, even when Wi-Fi or Bluetooth is off.” * Send usage and diagnostic data to Google * Google phone number verification * Google Gemini Apps Privacy Notice if you opt in to using Gemini Assistant * Google AI Prohibited Use Policy * Let contacts nearby find and share with you Other features, like Google Wallet, may require additional agreements. Final tally: four mandatory agreements and at least seven optional agreements. ---

articles.title: This tiny guitar amp is the most unhinged distortion pedal I’ve ever used
articles.summary: Death By Audio and Rainger FX’s Amp Crash is a tiny guitar amp, but it’s also the most unhinged distortion pedal I’ve ever used.
articles.body:
Is Amp Crash a guitar amp or a guitar pedal? Yes. Death By Audio’s latest is, in fact, both. While it’s in a guitar pedal enclosure, Amp Crash is actually a tiny 3-watt amp hooked up to a 2-inch speaker. You can even connect an external speaker if you want. This isn’t a digital re-creation of a classic Fender or Marshall like you might get from a Universal Audio amp sim pedal or a Neural DSP Cortex. This is an actual amp with an original design that moves air.  The tone you get out of this tiny thing is, unsurprisingly, harsh and boxy. But that’s not a criticism. Guitarists like Josh Homme (Queens of the Stone Age), Jack White, and Dan Auerbach (The Black Keys) have famously used cheap solid-state practice amps to get their unique tones. Amp Crash lives firmly in that realm. It never truly cleans up, even with the gain turned all the way down, and the brittle edge-of-overdrive at those lower settings has a charming, amateurish vibe. It’s not going to replace my Yamaha THR10, but I can’t hate on it. ---

--- What makes Amp Crash special, though, is that, in addition to a speaker, it also has a microphone inside. You can then feed the signal from that microphone into your digital audio workstation (DAW) or another amp, and capture the real sound of a speaker in a room being pushed to its limits. There’s a subtle magic that happens when the microphone picks up actual vibrations in the air and the sound of a room, instead of just running your guitar straight into Guitar Rig 7 in Ableton. And this is where Amp Crash’s real value lies, not as an amp, but as the world’s most convoluted distortion pedal.  The way the mic and speaker interact creates some truly wild sounds when you start cranking the gain. Once you turn the gain knob past 12 o’clock, it goes from crunchy, if slightly two-dimensional overdrive, to explosive fuzz. The tone knob at these higher gain settings has a huge impact, going from buzzsaw at the top to sludgy and uneasy at the bottom as the tiny speaker struggles to handle the bass frequencies. ---

--- Past three o’clock on the gain knob, things get truly insane as the speaker basically gives up. It flubs and rattles in a way that tells you it was not designed to take this level of abuse. But the mic also can’t keep up. It introduces its own crackles and clipping as it struggles to absorb the onslaught from the speaker. The introduced natural, slightly unpredictable compression turns your guitar into a brick wall of noise where the edges of individual notes and chords all collapse in on themselves. The two also create natural feedback so you can get that real cranked amp howl, without disturbing the neighbors too much. ---

--- You can dial in a bit of the direct signal (no mic) to add a bit of definition to your tone. Or even disable the speaker entirely by connecting a cable (no speaker) or a ¼-inch headphone adapter to the speaker-out jack. But why would you want to do that? Things get even more insane when you start playing with the small multi-effect module in the top right-hand corner of the pedal. You can choose between reverb, echo, or chorus. They’re all digital and quite lo-fi, with just two controls (depth and time) to play with. The chorus is rubbery and highly resonant, the echo crushed and self-oscillating, while the reverb is metallic and abrasive. ---

--- [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/268701_AmpCrash_-_this_guitar_amp_is_actually_the_craziest_distortion_pedal_TOBRIEN_DSCF0410.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] Add all these components together, and you get a little box that caters to the wildest of noisemakers. It’s no surprise that the companies that conceived of this thing are Death By Audio — the brainchild of Oliver Ackermann from noise rock mainstays A Place to Bury Strangers — and Rainger FX — a company that made a distortion pedal you fill with beer, soda, or even blood to change its tone. The Amp Crash is an appropriate addition to their legacy of musical chaos engines. [Media: https://youtu.be/SP2Uw5ahdzY]

articles.title: 'The Pitt' Season 3 trailer drops as more cast additions are revealed
articles.summary: The third installement of HBO Max’s Emmy-winning medical drama will premiere in January.
articles.body:
The third season of The Pitt isn't out until January, but a new teaser trailer for HBO Max's Emmy-winning medical drama was released on Friday, a day after more cast additions for the upcoming season were revealed.

The trailer shows star Noah Wylie's character, Dr. Robby, in the elevator on his first day back from a three-month sabbatical.

"I knew my first day back was gonna be hard dealing with what we go through here. And I knew that it could get a little bit crazy," he says in a dramatic voiceover. "But it's time to get back to it."

The series, which chronicles the challenges faced by health care professionals in the fictional emergency department of the Pittsburgh Trauma Medical Center, was nominated for 25 Emmy Awards this year — the most of any show on television.

According to Deadline , seven new actors will join the Noah Wyle-led ensemble as recurring guest stars: Stephen Chang ( Bosch: Legacy , The Last of Us: Part II ), Barry Clifton ( The Madison , The Thing About Pam ), Chris Diamantopoulos ( Dark Matter , The Lincoln Lawyer ), Lawrence Kao ( Criminal , Walker: Independence ), Brent Sexton ( Deadwood , The Madison ), JB Tadena ( The Adventures of Cliff Booth , Kung Fu ) and Hannah Ware ( The First , The One ).

That follows last month's announcement of six new additions to the recurring cast: Pruitt Taylor Vince ( Superman ), Malachi Beasley ( A House of Dynamite ), Cheyenne Perez ( The Sex Lives of College Girls ), Jeremy Radin ( The Accountant 2 ), Charlz Williams ( Seal Team ) and Rosanny Zayas ( The L Word: Generation Q ).

They'll all join the returning cast of Wyle, Katherine LaNasa, Sepideh Moafi, Patrick Ball, Isa Briones, Shawn Hatosy, Taylor Dearden, Fiona Dourif, Shabana Azeez, Gerran Howell and Ayesha Harris.

Wyle told Deadline that Season 3 is "about doctors benefiting from being patients. We're going to see that [Robby has] begun the therapeutic road; it's had a positive effect. It's fragile, and it's not without risk and vulnerability, but … at least there's forward progress."

The show, which follows a real-time format, will take place on Nov. 12, 2026.

Wylie also said the weather in Pittsburgh, Pa., where the show is set, would be a factor.

"You sort of turn the corner into fall, and those temperatures drop," he said. "All sorts of different kinds of cases come through the doors when you've got slick roads: people turning on their boilers and their heaters for the first time, house fires, the homeless situation where people are out on the street and cold. The weather is a character this season, for sure."

articles.title: Dreame’s dream of a rocket-powered car is dead
articles.summary: Dreame’s rocket-boosted car project is shutting down, after China’s government decided to take a harder look at the vacuum company’s ambitious ventures.
articles.body: Dreame, the Chinese vacuum company that aspires to be a global technology giant, is reportedly shutting down its automotive project after funding from the government dried up. According to CarNewsChina, the company’s automotive division called “Project Starry Sky” once employed over 1,000 people, but now only a handful legal and HR staffers remain, charged with winding down the operation. In a statement, Dreame said it “recently adjusted certain operations that were in the exploratory phase,” and that going forward, it would focus on four key business areas: “smart home, outdoor/garden, smart mobility, and embodied AI.” (A spokesperson for the company didn’t respond to a request for comment.) The news comes after China’s government issued new rules aimed at tightening oversight of the $3.4 trillion private fund industry, singling out Dreame in the process. After becoming one of the world’s largest manufacturer of vacuums, the company quickly moved into a variety of new businesses, spawning nearly a thousand affiliated ventures related to smartphones, robotics, and cars. But much of that expansion was funded by China’s government — and the government is now starting to take a closer look at how Dreame spends that money, according to CNBC. [Image: The NEXT 01 JET Edition Car at the Dreame NEXT event during the Silicon Valley Summit at the Palace of Fine Arts on April 29, 2026 in San Francisco, CA. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/05/268500_Dreame_NEXT_2026_KMcClellan_0068.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] Dreame wowed audiences at a San Francisco expo earlier this year with “Nebula Next 01 Jet Edition,” a sleek looking concept car equipped with a pair of rocket engines that theoretically can accelerate from 0 to 60 mph in 0.9 seconds. The vehicle was allegedly equipped with a sulfide-based solid-state battery with a record-breaking energy density exceeding 450 Wh/kg and a purported range of over 550 km (341.7 miles). The company claimed its boosters would deliver 100 kilo-Newtons of force. But the concept raised a lot of questions, including some basic ones about how Dreame could make a car accelerate so quickly without breaking the laws of physics. Apparently Dreame didn’t have any answers to these questions, as the car itself was fully vaporware. Former employees told China Economy that the concept that was shown off in San Francisco lacked an actual chassis and was driven via remote control. (Concept cars are rarely “real” cars, in the technical sense — but even this is a little shocking in its level of deception.) The news that Dreame’s vaporware car was totally vaporware will come as little shock to those familiar with the showy, boastful promises of companies that have never actually built a car suddenly deciding to build a car. Faraday Future, another Chinese companies with ambitions to build all manner of electric, autonomous vehicles, ran into this exact problem nearly a decade ago. And it also faced accusations of operating self-driving cars for public demos via offstage remote control.

articles.title: How Modern Appointment Viewing Shows Are Bringing Back ‘Watercooler’ Television
articles.summary: There’s nothing better than sitting on the couch to binge your favorite TV show. Or, maybe, there is. In the era of streaming, binge-watching is easier than...
articles.body:
There's nothing better than sitting on the couch to binge your favorite TV show. Or, maybe, there is. In the era of streaming, binge-watching is easier than ever. So, it seems potentially incongruous that appointment viewing — watching a television show when it first airs — is so capable of seizing the collective attention of viewers.

But fandom is a powerful force, and appointment viewing has tamed the beast into something fearsome. Rather than encouraging viewers to settle in with episode after episode queued up, shows like "Survivor," "The Pitt" and summer's guilty pleasure "Love Island" make their fans wait for it.

How 'The Pitt' Production Designer Expanded the Emergency Room for Season 2

'Survivor' vs. 'The Traitors': Will Emmy Voters Finally Give the Original Reality Juggernaut Its Due?

'The Pitt' Season 3 Trailer: Dr. Robby's First Day Back Is Filled With More Medical Emergencies

It's not a new concept; "Survivor" has been rocking weekly episode drops since its first foray in 2000 on the Bornean beaches. But it has reached a new fervor with watch parties popping up across the country and "Love Island'"s reality flair convincing millions to watch almost daily as hot singles couple up.

There's obvious incentive to watch when an episode airs if everyone is talking about it; you can hardly open your phone during "Love Island" season without seeing a spoiler. And the reality dating show takes it a step further: Fans can vote live on who must leave the villa and who lives to flirt another day.

"Survivor" has dabbled in the fan vote mechanism, too. An extra prize in "Survivor: All-Stars," casting selection for "Survivor: Cambodia — Second Chance" and gameplay elements in "Survivor 50: In the Hands of the Fans" were all left, well, in the hands of the fans.

Even a non-reality show like "The Pitt" has capitalized on the power behind scheduled releases. The first two episodes of Season 1 dropped concurrently on Jan. 9, 2025, but every subsequent episode has been released on a weekly schedule.

As with any show that received such critical esteem as the Pittsburgh-based medical drama, whose first season won five of its 13 Emmy nominations, Season 2 was accused online of a sophomore slump. Those critical social media fans were accused right back of not watching as intended (i.e., bandwagon binge-ing Season 1 and being upset about starting Season 2 before that was possible).

"Survivor" showrunner and Emmy-nominated host Jeff Probst describes the difference between binge-watching and appointment viewing as the difference between a flight and a road trip. Both get you to the destination, but with one, the time spent is part of the experience.

Viewers had a week to reckon with the knowledge that there was an active shooter event in the first season of "The Pitt" before the fallout reached the Pittsburgh Trauma Medical Center in the next episode. Skipping a night of "Love Island" this summer might have meant a fan's favorite couple exiting the villa — and certainly meant not understanding the social media memes and reactions the next day. Sure, you can binge old seasons of "Survivor," but you lose the emotional experience of living with Probst snuffing the torch of a beloved player.

The time between episodes is where fandom finds its home: reacting, interacting and generally causing a stir around a show in a way that binge-watches can't always pull off. "The Pitt" has been lauded as a return to classic television, the kind of "water cooler" show that inspires next-day conversations with coworkers.

"That waiting period creates a different kind of emotional investment because the audience begins supplying part of the experience," Probst says. Binge-watching builds momentum, but appointment viewing makes fans sit with the emotion.

Physical water coolers may be no more, but modern appointment viewing shows are fighting the impatience of binge watchers, and they're winning.

Skipping a night of "Love Island" this summer might have meant a fan's favorite couple exiting the villa — and certainly meant not understanding the social media memes and reactions the next day. Sure, you can binge old seasons of "Survivor," but you lose the emotional experience of living with Probst snuffing the torch of a beloved player.

The time between episodes is where fandom finds its home: reacting, interacting and generally causing a stir around a show in a way that binge-watches can't always pull off. "The Pitt" has been lauded as a return to classic television, the kind of "water cooler" show that inspires next-day conversations with coworkers.

"That waiting period creates a different kind of emotional investment because the audience begins supplying part of the experience," Probst says. Binge-watching builds momentum, but appointment viewing makes fans sit with the emotion.
Physical water coolers may be no more, but modern appointment viewing shows are fighting the impatience of binge watchers, and they're winning.
